Mortgage Products Are Not "One Size Fits All"

verifyText.value: There are a wide range of mortgage products available to meet the needs of your property and your specific financial need. For example, rates and terms can vary by:

Financial and mortgage regulations may differ from state to state. In addition, the status of property values, lending competition and local market conditions may result in different mortgage offers, rates and fees.
Typically, rates will vary between mortgages for a primary residence and those for a second or vacation home, mostly because of the risk associated with owning multiple homes.

The price of your home will help to determine whether it can be financed with a conforming, or conventional mortgage or a non-conforming "jumbo" mortgage. Jumbo mortgages tend to have slightly higher rates. The Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) publishes annual conforming loan limits that apply to all conventional mortgages delivered to Fannie Mae, including general loan limits and the high-cost area loan limits.
Mortgages with fewer years tend to have lower rates than longer term mortgages. And mortgages with adjustable rates tend to be lower (at least initially) than fixed rate mortgages.
The Relationship Between Years And Rates

waitForText.value: The Relationship Between Years And Rates

verifyText.value: In general, the more time you have to repay what you borrow, the higher "price" - the interest rate - you will be asked to pay for that loan. Rates on 30-year mortgages tend to be slightly higher than 15-year mortgage rates.
Simply put, the longer you pay, the more in interest you will pay.

If you happen to sell your home in just a few years from now, you might pay more in interest with a 30-year loan than a 15-year loan. This is because mortgages are structured so that interest payments are "front-loaded" in the early repayment years. This means, initially, most of each monthly payment is applied to pay interest, while only a very small portion goes to repay the principal (the amount borrowed). Gradually, over time, the portion applied to repay principal increases.
Keep in mind your cash flow
Although a 15-year mortgage rate may be lower than a 30-year mortgage rate, the compressed repayment period will create larger monthly payments.

Your FICO score (an acronym for the credit scoring service, Fair Isaacs Company) is an assigned number between 300 and 850 that indicates to lenders your capacity to repay a loan. It can change regularly, as new information is sent by your creditors to one or more of the three major national credit bureaus, Experian, Trans Union, and Equifax. The higher your FICO score, the more likely you will qualify for a mortgage loan and the best interest rates.
A FICO score is comprised of 5 parts:

Your types of accounts and your payment record; any bankruptcies, legal judgments, wage garnishments, etc.; the severity and amount of late payments; the number of past-due items and when they occurred. (35%)
How much you currently owe and on what types of accounts; number of accounts with balances; the proportion of credit lines still available. (30%)
Time since accounts opened; by specific type of account; since last activity. (15%)
Number of recently opened accounts, by type and date opened; recent credit inquiries and date of inquiries; reestablishment of good credit after payment delinquencies. (10%)
The number and types of credit accounts available for your use. (10%)
By federal law, you're entitled to a free credit report once every 12 months from each of the three major credit bureaus - Experian, TransUnion, or Equifax.

verifyText.value: Picking The Best Mortgage For You

waitForText.value: Picking The Best Mortgage For You

verifyText.value: Choosing the mortgage with the best fit for you may feel complicated, but you can make it simpler by focusing on which of the following factors is most important to you: Lower the monthly payment You might allocate cash to increase the points (or upfront interest rate charges), which will lower the interest rate, which in turn will lower the monthly payment. You might increase your down payment, which will lower the loan amount, and in turn, the monthly payment. A longer-term mortgage, say 30 years instead of 15, will lower the monthly payments, even if it increases the total cost of the loan over the life of the mortgage. Consider an adjustable rate mortgage or ARM that typically offer more affordable monthly payments during the initial fixed interest period. However, be careful not to set yourself up for future payment shock you can't afford if the rate adjusts higher later on.

Shorter-term mortgages generally mean repaying larger portions of principal with each monthly payment. So, if you want to pay off your mortgage more rapidly, and can tolerate a higher monthly payment, you may want to compare mortgages of different terms.
To conserve current cash, you might choose a mortgage with fewer points and see how much higher your interest rate and payment will go as a trade-off.
